pages.text: Britain's Bonfire Night Events Worth Traveling For | National Geographic TRAVEL Britain's Bonfire Night Events Worth Traveling For Get winter off to a cracking start with our pick of the November festivities, from fireworks in London to flaming tar barrels in Devon. This raucous, torch-lit parade in Lewes features brass bands, bagpipes and firecrackers as well as a procession of giant, caricature effigies. Photograph by Sussex News; Alamy By Orla Thomas Last updated November 1, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). ‘Remember, remember, the fifth of November’, goes the old nursery rhyme, ‘gunpowder, treason and plot.’ It’s a memorably succinct summary of the events of that very night in 1605, when Catholic rebel Guy Fawkes tried to blow up the Houses of Parliament and assassinate England’s Protestant king, James I. The monarch’s survival has been marked ever since and celebrations have evolved over the centuries. Traditionally, Guy’s effigy was burned on bonfires across the land, but now fireworks are the most common means of commemorating his failed — yet infamous — explosives attempt. Whichever event you choose, snack on beloved seasonal accompaniments — such as baked potatoes or toffee apples — as the dark skies over Britain become a blaze of colour. The tradition of carrying burning, tar-coated barrels through the streets of Ottery St Mary in Devon is a centuries-old tradition. Photograph by Steve Davey Photography; Alamy 1. The official sign on the banks of the River Tone at French Weir Park in Taunton advises people not to swim. But that hasn't stopped Jo, Jenny, Sue and a second Jo from enjoying a regular dip together. "People think, oh you're swimming down by the supermarket, that can't be very nice, but it's gorgeous," Jenny Hillier says, as the women huddle round with their coats and hot drinks after a bracing October plunge. People have been swimming at the spot on the River Tone in the centre of Taunton for more than a hundred years. But it is only since 2024 that French Weir Park has been designated an official bathing site, which means from May to September the water gets tested by the Environment Agency (EA). Those tests regularly confirm what the women's senses have been telling them for a while - the water quality is poor. "There are times when we've come down and we haven't got in, either because of the look or the smell," says Jo Macdonald. "We don't take risks. We don't put our faces in. The Boeing 787 Dreamliner bound for Lagos in Nigeria became stuck after its front wheel entered the grass as it was taxiing independently from the gate to the runway shortly after 10:00 GMT. A spokesperson for the west London airport said they were continuing to assist the plane back to the aircraft parking area, adding that there were no injuries and no impact on wider operations. A spokesperson for BA said: "We're very sorry to our customers for the disruption to their flight. All the passengers disembarked safely and efforts to extract the aircraft are still taking place. The man, who has not been identified, landed at RAF Northolt before being transported to a specialist infectious diseases unit at the Royal Free Hospital in north London. It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths. Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of the All Hazards Public Health Response team at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), said there are "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and the risk to the public remains low. What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? The infected doctor was brought to the UK on a medical evacuation flight as part of a joint effort by the UK and DR Congo governments and their international health partners, the Department of Health (DoH) said. pages.text: Broadmead Road Bridge: How a broken crossing has split a community Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live How a broken London bridge has split a community 4 days ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Karl Mercer London political editor, in Woodford BBC Broadmead Road Bridge has been closed to all but pedestrians, bikes and motorcycles for more than three years The deserted and slightly forlorn bus stop will give you a clue that all is not well with Broadmead Road Bridge in Woodford, north-east London. There hasn't been a bus here for more than three years - or for that matter a car, a lorry or a van. Safety concerns led to the bridge, which crosses the Central line, being closed in July 2023. Financial concerns mean it hasn't yet been fixed. The local council, Redbridge, says it can't afford the £100m it would take, so has asked the government to step in. It's put in a bid to something called the structures fund - a £1bn pot of money the Department for Transport (DfT) has for infrastructure schemes that authorities across the country can apply for. It's due to announce who will be awarded funds soon. Council leader Kam Rai says Redbridge needs government help to rebuild the bridge Graffiti on the abandoned bus stop reads "Never back down, never give up", perhaps a suitable message for Redbridge Council leader Kam Rai as he waits to hear if the borough's latest bid for help has worked. pages.text: Bronze Age Akrotiri Is Greek's Pompeii Skip to main content History | November 3, 2026 Greece Has Its Own Pompeii, and the Ruins Tell a Captivating Story of a Sophisticated, Seafaring Bronze Age Society The Thera volcano, on modern-day Santorini, buried Akrotiri in ash in the 17th or 16th century B.C.E. The eruption was one of the largest in recorded history The ruins of Akrotiri, a Bronze Age settlement on what is now the Greek island of Santorini Westend61 via Getty Images The ruins of Akrotiri, a Bronze Age settlement on what is now the Greek island of Santorini Westend61 via Getty Images The earth rumbled for days. Inhabitants of the seafaring Bronze Age settlement of Akrotiri watched smoke plume from Thera , a long-dormant volcano on what is now the Greek island of Santorini . People gathered their belongings and safely stored the valuables they were forced to leave behind. Then they fled by boat to nearby islands. When these minor earthquakes and eruptions subsided, residents returned to Akrotiri, collecting materials for reconstruction and beginning the arduous process of repairing the damage . But the ground continued to tremble. As conditions worsened , they made the difficult decision to flee once more, hopeful that their homes would survive the coming devastation. When Thera erupted again, the explosion was so powerful that it destroyed Akrotiri, burying the settlement (and the island that shared the volcano’s name) in some 200 feet of ash and pumice stone. What themes and melodies spoke to the past can easily echo into the present, but come alive through the personality of its interpreter. Brìghde Chaimbeul expands the language of the Scottish smallpipes behind the Desk with a quiet, yet demonstrative presence. Chaimbeul grew up on the Isle of Skye, Scotland, speaking Gaelic and learning the Highland pipes before falling in love with the bellows-blown bagpipe she plays today. Drones are forever with this instrument, but Chaimbeul amplifies, manipulates and darkens the harmonics and frequencies of these pipe drones with effects pedals and contact mics that capture her percussive tapping on the chanter. The effect is mystic and ancient … completely transfixing. But if you have diabetes, these events can pose special challenges to your meal plan. By using these buffet tips and choosing food wisely, you can still have a delicious meal, feel good, and have some fun! General tips Plan which foods you want to limit before you go. Also, think about which foods will help you manage your blood sugar. Check all the options on the buffet before you serve yourself. Then choose one or two favorite treats along with healthier items to round out your meal. Watch your portions. However, many of these structures do not meet current building code requirements and require strategic upgrades. To address this vulnerability, NIST is actively developing best practices, design recommendations, and guidelines for utilizing building retrofit systems to improve the performance of existing structures. Beyond individual structures, it is critical to understand how different retrofit schemes and targets impact the community recovery. NIST is leading ongoing projects to quantify and measure the impact of various retrofit strategies at the community level. By developing the fundamental measurement science needed to assess retrofitted building performance, this work directly supports the long-term resilience and rapid recovery of communities following natural hazards. For millennia, people have suffered from bunions, a painful condition that’s uniquely human. Here’s why—and how to ease the pain. A colored x-ray image highlights bunions in the feet of a 54-year-old patient. The foot deformity may affect up to a quarter of the modern adult population. ZEPHYR/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY By Erin Blakemore Last updated October 14, 2025 Bunions have plagued human feet since ancient times. A brief glimpse at archaeology and history points to their presence, from prehistoric footprints in England to ancient Egyptian mummies with bony bumps . A whopping 27 percent of burials in and around Cambridge, England, during the 14th and 15th centuries showed skeletal evidence of bunions, compared with just 6 percent in earlier centuries. The likely culprit? Researchers attribute the difference to the medieval emergence of “poulaine” shoes , long leather footwear with a pointed tip. But why do we get them in the first place—and why haven’t we figured out how they’re caused or cured without surgery? pages.text: Business Dynamics Statistics of Human Capital (BDS-HC) Business Dynamics Statistics of Human Capital (BDS-HC) Business Dynamics Statistics of Human Capital (BDS-HC) September 2026 The Business Dynamics Statistics of Human Capital (BDS-HC) is an experimental data product that extends the set of statistics published by the Business Dynamics Statistics program. These are the first public-use statistics that use W-2 filings to combine longitudinal business data with population-level worker demographic data to classify firms based on the characteristics of their workers. The BDS-HC tables describe the relationship between business dynamics and workforce composition for nearly all non-farm employer businesses in the United States from 2000 to 2023. Each table reports all economic outcomes covered by the BDS, including establishment openings and closings, firm startups and shutdowns, and job creation and destruction, for different groups of firms based on their workforce composition. Separate tables are available based on the share of a firm’s workforce that belongs to each category within six demographic characteristics: age, sex, race, ethnicity, nativity, and education. Tables also provide statistics broken out by the interaction between workforce composition and business characteristics, such as the establishment’s industrial sector and state and the firm’s size and age. The BDS-SU-REV provides year-over-year changes in employment, payroll, and revenue for each quarter of the year for businesses that operate in one location (single-units) and file their taxes under a single Employer Identification Number (EIN). This product relies on IRS annual tax filings to collect revenue information and IRS quarterly tax filings to collect employment and payroll information for the pay periods including March 12 th , June 12 th , September 12 th , and December 12 th . Year-over-year employment and payroll changes are calculated between the same point in year t and year t-1 (i.e., June 12 th year t-1 to June 12 th year t, etc.). Employment and payroll growth is labeled as job and pay creation respectively and employment and payroll decline as job and pay destruction. A novel innovation in the BDS-SU-REV is the incorporation of annual revenue data for single-establishment firms that consistently maintain positive employment levels each quarter. A positive annual growth in revenue is categorized as revenue creation, while negative growth is categorized as revenue destruction. Jump to: Data Definitions

The survey provides local, state, and federal officials near real-time data for policy and decision-making including after natural disasters or during economic crises. The BTOS also provides insights into business recovery after these events. The BTOS sample consists of approximately 1.2 million businesses split into six panels (approximately 200,000 cases per panel). Businesses in each panel are asked to report once every 12 weeks over the course of one year. Data collection occurs every two weeks. The BTOS is comprised of a set of core questions and supplemental content, which is added as needed. The BTOS collects information on a broad range of business conditions. Topics include current performance, changes in revenue, employment, hours worked, demand, and prices. For most concepts, businesses are asked about the previous two weeks and for a 6-month outlook. Data collected from September 11, 2023 to present include all employer businesses (single location and multi-location) in the U.S. economy, excluding farms. pages.title: But I'm a Cheerleader | Movies | The Guardian
pages.description: Peter Bradshaw: Reasonably amusing, with 2-D acting and writing, and Day-Glo pink and blue colour schemes.
pages.text: But I'm a Cheerleader | Movies | The Guardian Skip to main content Skip to navigation Movies This article is more than 25 years old Review But I'm a Cheerleader This article is more than 25 years old Peter Bradshaw Thu 12 Apr 2001 21.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google D irector and co-writer Jamie Babbit makes her feature debut with this satire of America's creepy Christian "sexual reorientation" camps, where confused teens are sent so that their nascent gayness can be deprogrammed out of them. Natasha Lyonne plays Megan, a cheerleader who hugs her fellow pom-pom-botherers inappropriately and hates making out with her jock boyfriend. He and Megan's family arrange an "intervention" where she is confronted with her shameful tendencies and sent to the True Directions camp, run by two smug tyrants in Straight Is Great T-shirts, played by Cathy Moriarty and RuPaul (here out of drag), clearly repressed gays themselves. Once there, Megan falls for a girl with the interesting name of Graham, played by Clea DuVall. As in all therapy boot-camp movies - such as Girl, Interrupted, in which DuVall had a role - there has to be a wild child with whom the heroine makes a connection. This is Graham's role. It's reasonably amusing, with 2-D acting and writing, and Day-Glo pink and blue colour schemes. But it could have been funnier, and I would have preferred to know more in documentary terms about the actual reality of these terrible camps, rather than sit through this heavy-handed and oddly lenient comedy. pages.text: Buying a Train Ticket | National Rail Skip to main content Buying a Ticket Find the best train ticket for you Want to know what ticket types are available, how much they cost, and where and when you can buy and use them? Then read on. Which train ticket is the best choice for me? As a general rule, the earlier you can buy a ticket, the better the price you can get. If you know the date and time you wish to travel, then an Advance ticket will be suitable. For more flexibility, Off-Peak and Super Off-Peak tickets and Anytime tickets will be a better option, as you are not limited to a specific date or train. For more information about getting the most affordable ticket for your journey, see below. Advance tickets These must be bought in advance and are only valid on the date and train specified. They are sold in limited numbers, subject to availability and on a first come, first served basis. You can usually buy an Advance ticket up to 12 weeks ahead of travel, and they are still available until the day of travel on many routes – sometimes up to 10 minutes before departure. They offer a great deal if you know exactly when you want to travel. Find out more about Advance tickets . Off-Peak and Super Off-Peak tickets These good value tickets can be bought at any time and allow you to travel on any permitted train during off-peak hours. If an Off-Peak or Super Off-Peak ticket is available for your journey, journey planners will make them available to purchase. In general, Off-Peak hours begin at 09:30 from Monday to Friday in cities and large towns, and at 09:00 everywhere else.

pages.title: By Land and Sea—17 European Trips From London | National Geographic
pages.description: Whether it’s a short hop across the Channel or an overland expedition to the furthest reaches of Europe, some of the richest travel experiences happen when you skip the flight.
pages.text: By Land and Sea—17 European Trips From London | National Geographic By Oliver Smith Published October 24, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Today, it’s easier to travel further and faster around Europe than ever before — to board a flight and effectively parachute yourself into a new destination. But by travelling overland, be it by ferry, train or car, on a bike or on foot, you’re able to observe the slow, subtle changes at ground level with every accumulated mile. Overland travel by rail is also easier than it’s ever been, thanks to an ever-expanding network of high-speed and sleeper trains across Europe. You might board a morning Eurostar at London St Pancras International and that same day be joining a midnight crawl of Madrid’s tapas bars or standing beneath Milan’s hulking Duomo as stars twinkle above its white marble facade. Ferries, too, offer perspectives unfamiliar to those at the cruising altitude of an airliner, whether that’s witnessing the green coast of northern Spain unravelling out of the blue horizons of Biscay or seeing Icelandic volcanoes peek over grey North Atlantic waves. DOE supports the development, standardization, and maintenance of calibration facilities for environmental radiation sensors. Radiation standards at the facilities are primarily used to calibrate portable surface gamma-ray survey meters and borehole logging instruments used for uranium and other mineral exploration and remedial action measurements. Standards for calibrating borehole fission neutron devices are also available, but are used infrequently. Radiation standards are constructed of concrete with elevated, uniform concentrations of naturally occurring potassium, uranium, and/or thorium. Pad standards have large, flat surfaces suitable for calibration measurements with portable surface survey meters. Borehole standards are large concrete cylinders with 4.5-inch-diameter test holes. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/calibration-services Standards Calibration services Sign Up to Get NIST News GovDelivery Purchase calibrations Learn more about calibrations NIST on a Chip If you need to measure something, NIST is the go-to place for help. And NIST is also the place to go if you need to calibrate your measuring equipment. In our everyday lives, calibrations are often the little adjustments you may make, for example to make sure the colors of your computer monitor or television are accurate, so it will show photos or videos the way that a filmmaker or photographer intended. But for a scientific measurement laboratory such as NIST, calibrations are a bit different. NIST calibrations determine a relationship between the measurement standard (like the Kibble balance) and that instrument or object (such as a cylindrical metal kilogram mass). By using a world-class reference such as the Kibble balance, calibrations make it possible for a piece of measuring equipment to make the most accurate measurement it can. From MRIs to lasers, NIST's calibration services are part of many aspects of everyday life.
